title: Native AOT and memory
sub: The same collector, no JIT, data in the image
cards/0/body:
A regular .NET app ships as IL, and the JIT turns methods into machine code while it runs. Native AOT (ahead-of-time) does that at publish time: the ILC compiler takes the IL of the whole app along with its libraries and produces a single native executable.

The runtime does not go away. A compact runtime is baked into the file: the garbage collector, exceptions, threads, type handling. What is missing is the JIT and everything needed to load and compile IL.

Native AOT is available for console apps since .NET 7 and for ASP.NET Core (minimal APIs, gRPC) since .NET 8.
cards/0/code:
<!-- in the .csproj -->
<PropertyGroup>
    <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
</PropertyGroup>

# publish for a specific platform
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64
cards/0/deep: Native AOT descends from the CoreRT and .NET Native (UWP) projects. Its runtime lives in dotnet/runtime under src/coreclr/nativeaot. Before it there was ReadyToRun (crossgen): it also compiles ahead of time, but keeps the IL and the JIT — for recompilation and for whatever could not be precompiled. Native AOT goes all the way: there is no IL in the output.
cards/1/title: The collector is the very same
cards/1/body:
The key point for this course: Native AOT runs the same collector, built from the same sources as in regular CoreCLR. So everything from the previous units still holds:

  • generations 0, 1, 2, the LOH and the POH;
  • the fast allocation path through the thread’s context and the slow path;
  • Workstation and Server, background GC, latency modes;
  • pinning, finalization, weak references.

Settings work the same way too: project properties (ServerGarbageCollection, ConcurrentGarbageCollection) and DOTNET_* environment variables. There is just no separate runtimeconfig.json next to the app — the project values go into the executable itself at publish time.
cards/1/deep: An allocation costs the same in AOT: new is the same pointer bump in the thread’s context. The differences are in the details around it: for example, AOT has no tiered compilation, and so no Dynamic PGO — in the regular runtime the JIT sometimes removes allocations using profile data (devirtualization, stack allocation), while AOT code is compiled once and without a profile.
cards/2/q: A service was moved to Native AOT. The load and the set of objects are the same. What happens to GC pauses?
cards/2/options/0: Roughly the same: the collector and the heap work the same way
cards/2/options/1: They disappear: Native AOT has no garbage collector
cards/2/options/2: They grow: AOT code allocates twice as much
cards/2/options/3: Gen 2 collections disappear: the heap does not age in AOT
cards/2/explain: Native AOT removes the JIT, not the collector. A pause depends on live objects, roots and the GC mode — none of that changed. Want fewer pauses — fewer allocations and live objects, same as without AOT.
cards/3/body:
Native AOT saves not on the heap but on everything around it in a regular process:

  • no JIT — the compiler itself is not loaded, and neither is its working memory;
  • no code heap — in the regular runtime generated machine code sits in memory allocated by the process, often in two versions (tier 0 and tier 1);
  • no loading of IL and metadata — type structures are already built by the compiler and stored in the file;
  • fast startup — nothing to compile, the first request does not wait for the JIT.

Code and type data are mapped from the file as image pages (as in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit): they are read-only and shared between processes of the same file.
cards/3/deep: How much smaller depends on the app: for small services the working set difference can be several-fold, for services with gigabyte heaps it is within noise, because data takes most of the memory there. The flip side is file size: it contains all the library code that is used. That is why ILC aggressively trims everything unreachable.
cards/4/q: Which memory disappears or shrinks noticeably under Native AOT? Select all.
cards/4/options/0: The memory of the JIT compiler itself
cards/4/options/1: Code generated by the JIT at run time
cards/4/options/2: The managed heap with your objects
cards/4/options/4: Type structures the runtime builds while loading IL
cards/4/explain: The heap and stacks work the same: there are as many objects and threads as the program creates. What goes away is everything tied to compiling and loading IL at run time.
cards/5/title: Frozen objects: data right in the image
cards/5/body:
Some objects in Native AOT are never created at run time at all. The compiler lays them out in the file ready-made, with a header and a type pointer — these are frozen objects:

  • string literals — every string from the code already sits in the image;
  • precomputed static data — if a static constructor is simple, ILC runs it at build time and writes the result into the file.

The collector neither moves nor collects such objects: they are not in its heap. You can reference them like any other object.
cards/5/deep: Regular CoreCLR has something similar since .NET 8: string literals, RuntimeType objects for typeof and Array.Empty<T>() are placed in a separate non-GC heap (NonGC heap). The JIT bakes their address straight into machine code, and GC.GetGeneration returns int.MaxValue for them. More on frozen segments in the "Inside the heap" unit.
cards/6/q: Native AOT. Where does each thing end up?
cards/6/pairs/0/1: A frozen object in the executable
cards/7/body:
No JIT means nothing that generates code at run time:

  • System.Reflection.Emit and dynamic assemblies — PlatformNotSupportedException;
  • loading assemblies from files at run time;
  • Expression.Compile() and RegexOptions.Compiled work, but through an interpreter;
  • reflection sees only what survived trimming: the compiler flags risky spots with IL2xxx and IL3xxx warnings.

For memory this means: serializers and DI containers that used to generate code on the fly switch to source generators under AOT. The code is produced at compile time, and no run-time memory goes into building and caching generated methods.
cards/7/deep: Another consequence: generics. Each List<T> with a value-type T needs its own machine code, and ILC has to see all such instantiations at build time. A MakeGenericType(typeof(MyStruct)) the compiler did not foresee fails at run time. For reference-type T the code is shared (as in the "Generics" unit of the "Deeper C#" course), so there are fewer problems with them.
cards/8/q: The app is published with PublishAot. Which line throws PlatformNotSupportedException?
cards/8/explain: Creating a dynamic assembly means generating IL at run time, and under AOT there is nobody to run it: there is no JIT. The compiler warns about this spot in advance (IL3050). The other lines are ordinary code known at build time.
cards/9/body:
Before switching to AOT, measure both versions under the same load:

  • time to first response — AOT almost always wins here;
  • peak RSS / working set — at startup and under load;
  • steady-state throughput — here the JIT with Dynamic PGO may turn out faster;
  • GC counters — the number of collections and pauses should nearly match.

Where AOT pays off: short-lived processes (CLIs, serverless), dense container packing, cold start. Where the gain is small: a long-running service with a big heap.
cards/9/code:
# Linux: peak RSS over the whole process lifetime
/usr/bin/time -v ./app 2>&1 | grep "Maximum resident"

# GC counters of a live process
dotnet-counters monitor -n app --counters System.Runtime
cards/9/deep: Diagnostics support in AOT is narrower than in the regular runtime and depends on the version. EventPipe (which dotnet-counters and dotnet-trace rely on) has to be enabled in an AOT app at build time with the EventSourceSupport property, and analyzing dumps with SOS is not supported for AOT processes. Before switching, check which tools from the "How to measure" unit you are going to use.
cards/10/q: Put in order the path from sources to a running AOT process
cards/10/items/1: ILC builds the graph of reachable code and trims the rest
cards/10/items/2: ILC compiles methods to machine code and lays out frozen data
cards/10/items/3: The linker combines the code and the runtime with its collector into one file
cards/10/items/4: At startup the collector creates the heap; no JIT is loaded
cards/10/explain: First a regular compilation to IL, then ILC: trimming, generating code and data. The system linker binds everything with the runtime. At startup the heap is created as usual — via reserve and commit, as in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit.
cards/11/q: For which app will Native AOT save the most memory?
cards/11/options/0: A CLI tool that is run hundreds of times a day for seconds
cards/11/options/1: A service with a 20 GB cache that runs for weeks
cards/11/options/2: An app that builds proxies with Reflection.Emit
cards/11/options/3: A batch job that holds big arrays in the LOH for a month
cards/11/explain: For a short process the main cost is startup and the runtime’s fixed overhead: the JIT, code, metadata. AOT removes exactly those. In the 20 GB cache service and the batch job data takes the memory, and Reflection.Emit does not work under AOT at all.
